Recall that an edge is present between $u$ and $v$ with probability
$$
\text{Edge probability} = \frac{\kappa(u, v)}{n}.
$$

$$
\begin{align*}
a(1-b) + b(1-a)
& = b(1-b) \frac{a}{b} + a(1-a) \frac{b}{a} \\
& = \frac{b(1-b) a^2}{ab} + \frac{a(1-a) b^2}{ab} \\
& = \frac{b a^2 - b^2 a^2 + ab^2 - a^2 b^2}{ab} \\
& = \frac{a - 2 b a + b}{ab} \\
& \leq \frac{2 \max - 2 \min}{ab}
\end{align*}
$$




$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{P} \left( \mathbf 1_{\{\{x, y\} \in e(G(n, \kappa))\}} \neq \mathbf 1_{\{\{A_m^x, A_m^y\} \in e(G(n, \overline{\kappa}_m))\}} \right)
& = a(1-b) + b(1-a)
&& a \, \colon = \frac{\kappa}{n}, b \, \colon = \frac{\overline{\kappa}}{n}\\
& \leq 2 \max(a,b) - 2 \min(a,b)  \\
& \leq \frac{2 \varepsilon_m}{n}.
\end{align*}
$$

$$
\begin{align*}
\pi_{m(n)}^t
& = \frac{1}{\tilde \lambda_{m(n)} + 1} \int_{\mathcal S} \kappa(s, t) \mu_{m(n)}^t(s) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \pi_{m(n)}(s)
&& \text{p. } 591 \\
& = \frac{\mu_{m(n)}^t}{\tilde \lambda_{m(n)} + 1} \int_{\mathcal S} \kappa(s, t) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \pi_{m(n)}(s) \\
& \leq \frac{\sup_{n, x, y} \kappa_n(x, y) \cdot\mu_{m(n)}^t}{\tilde \lambda_{m(n)} + 1}  \int_{\mathcal S} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \pi_{m(n)}(s) \\

\end{align*}
$$

::: {.card title="p607_final"}

By definition, we have

$$
\begin{align*}
(\tilde \lambda + 1) \cdot \pi(t)
& = \int_{\mathcal S} \kappa(s, t) \mu(t) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \pi(s) \\
& = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{s=1}^{M_{m(n)}}
    \overline \kappa_{m(n)}(s, t) \mu(A_{m(n)t}) \pi(A_{m(n)s}). \\
\end{align*}
$$


This leads to

$$
\begin{align*}
\tilde \lambda + 1
& = \frac{1}{\pi(t)} \cdot
    \int_{\mathcal S} \kappa(s, t) \mu(t) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \pi(s) \\
& = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{\pi(A_{m(n)t})} \cdot \sum_{s=1}^{M_{m(n)}}
    \overline \kappa_{m(n)}(s, t) \mu(A_{m(n)t}) \pi(A_{m(n)s}). \\
& = \lim_{n \to \infty} \tilde \lambda_{m(n)} + 1 \\
& = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{ \pi_{m(n)} (t) } \cdot \sum_{s=1}^{M_{m(n)}}
    \overline \kappa_{m(n)}(s, t) \mu_{m(n)}(t) \pi_{m(n)}(s).
&& \mu_{m(n)}(t) \, \colon = \mu(A_{m(n)t})
\end{align*}
$$

By uniqueness of $\pi_{m(n)}$, the equality between the second and last expression above implies that



$$
\pi_{m(n)}(t) = \pi(A_{m(n)t}).
$$ {#eq-piMN}


We now have the tools to explain why

$$
\sum_{s \in \mathcal S_{m(n)}} \frac{\pi_{m(n)} (s) ^ 2}{\mu_{m(n)}(s)}
\xrightarrow{n \to \infty}
\int_{\mathcal S} \frac{\pi(s)}{\mu(s)} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \pi(s).
$$


Indeed

$$
\begin{align*}
\int_{\mathcal S} \frac{\pi(s)}{\mu(s)} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \pi(s)
& = \lim_{n \to \infty}
    \sum_{s=1}^{M_{m(n)}}
    \frac{\pi(A_{m(n)s})}{\mu(A_{m(n)s})} \pi(A_{m(n)s})
&& \text{by definition of the integral} \\
& = \lim_{n \to \infty}
    \sum_{s \in \mathcal S_{m(n)}}
    \frac{\pi_{m(n)}(s)}{\mu_{m(n)}(s)} \pi_{m(n)}(s) \\
& = \lim_{n \to \infty}
    \sum_{s \in \mathcal S_{m(n)}}
    \frac{\pi_{m(n)}(s) ^ 2}{\mu_{m(n)}(s)}.
\end{align*}
$$


Where we used (@eq-piMN) to go from the first to the second line.

:::

::: {.card title="dense setting proof"}

Recall that a kernel $\kappa$ is homogeneous if

$$
\int_{\mathcal S} \kappa(s, t) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \mu(t) = 1
\quad \text{for a.e. } s \in \mathcal S.

$$


$$
\tilde \lambda_n \to \infty \, + \, 
\kappa \text{ is a homogeneous kernel} \implies
\text{Dense setting.}
$$

$$
\eta_{st}^n \sim \text{Binomial}
\left( n_t - \delta_{st}, \frac{\kappa_n(s, t)}{n} \right)
$$

$$
\begin{align*}
\implies \mathrm{E} \left[ \eta_{st}^n \right] 
& = \kappa_n(s,t) \cdot \frac{(n_t - \delta_{st})}{n} \\
& \xrightarrow{p} \kappa_n(s,t) \cdot \mu(t)

\end{align*}
$$
$$
\begin{align*}
&\mathrm{E} \left[ \eta_{st}^n \right] 
&& \approx \int_{\mathcal S} \kappa_n(s,t) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \mu(t)
&& \text{assumption 1} \\
&&& = \tilde \lambda_n + 1
&& \text{homogeneous kernel} \\
&&& \to \infty, \\
&\mathrm{E} \left[ \eta_{st}^n \right] 
&& \approx \int_{\mathcal S} \kappa_n(s,t) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \mu(t)
&& \text{assumption 2} \\
&&& = (\tilde \lambda_n + 1) 
      \int_{\mathcal S} \kappa(s,t) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \mu(t)
&& \kappa_n = (\tilde \lambda_n + 1) \cdot\kappa \\
&&& \geq (\tilde \lambda_n + 1)  \cdot c
&& \text{integral striclty greater than constant } c > 0 \\ 
&&& \to \infty.
\end{align*}
$$

Time between two consecutive splits given the number N of alive particles after the first of these two splits: minimum of N independent EXP(1) random variables.

Recall that the minimum of N independent exponential random variables with the ith of these random variables having parameter $\lambda_i$ is ALSO distributed as an exponential random variable but with parameter $\sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i$. Since

$$
\mathrm{E} \left[ \text{Exp}(\lambda) \right] = \frac{1}{\lambda},
$$
$$
\mathrm{E} \left[ \min_{i=1}^N \text{Exp}(\lambda_i) \right] = \frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i}.
$$
Recall that $D_j^n$ denotes the number of children produced at the moment the jth particle dies.

$$
D_j^n \sim \text{Poisson} \left( \int_{\mathcal S} 
\kappa_n(\text{type of node } j, t) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \mu(t)\right)
\stackrel{\kappa_n \text{ homogeneous}}{=}
\text{Poisson} \left( \tilde \lambda_n + 1 \right).
$$

$$
\begin{align*}
D_j^n 
& \sim \text{Poisson} \left( \int_{\mathcal S} 
\kappa_n(\text{type of node } j, t) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \mu(t)\right) \\
& = \text{Poisson} \left( (\tilde \lambda_n + 1) 
\int_{\mathcal S} \kappa(\text{type of node } j, t) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \mu(t) \right).
\end {align*}
$$

$$
\begin{align*}
S_i^n 
&=&&\text{number of children born up to and including the ith split } - \\
&&&\text{number of particles that have died up to and including the ith split } +\\
&&&\text{the original particle a.k.a. the source particle} \\
&=&&\sum_{j=1}^i D_j^n - i + 1.

\end{align*}
$$
CLT:

$$
\frac
  {\sum_{i\in[n]} X_i - n \mathrm{E} \left[ X \right]}
  {\sqrt{  \mathrm{Var} \left[ X \right] n }}
\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(0,1).
$$

CLT applied to $X \sim \text{Poisson}$

$$
\begin{align*}
\frac
  {\sum_{j\in[i]} D_j^n - i (\tilde \lambda_n + 1)} 
  {\sqrt{i (\tilde \lambda_n + 1)}}
& \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(0,1). \\
\frac
  {\sum_{j\in[i]} D_j^n - i (\tilde \lambda_n + 1)} 
  {\sqrt{i (\tilde \lambda_n + 1)}}
& = \frac
  {S_i^n - i \tilde \lambda_n - 1} 
  {\sqrt{i (\tilde \lambda_n + 1)}} \\
& = 
\frac
  {S_i^n - i \tilde \lambda_n} 
  {\sqrt{i (\tilde \lambda_n + 1)}} -
\frac
  {1} 
  {\sqrt{i (\tilde \lambda_n + 1)}}
\implies \\
\frac
  {S_i^n - i \tilde \lambda_n} 
  {\sqrt{i (\tilde \lambda_n + 1)}}
& \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(0,1). \\
\end{align*}
$$


Recall that the sum of independent Poisson random variables is Poisson distributed with the new parameter being the sum of the parameters. Thus,

$$
\sum_{j\in[i]} D_j^n \sim
\text{Poisson} \left(
  (\tilde \lambda_n + 1)
  \sum_{j\in[i]} \int_{\mathcal S} \kappa(\text{type of node } j, t) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \mu(t)
\right).
$$


The Lindeberg condition then allows us to use the CLT event though the $D_j^n$s are not identically distributed.
